payload.original: Historical investigation recorded from primary sources. During the Plugs-Out Integrated Test of spacecraft 012 at Launch Complex 34 on 27 January 1967, a fire in the 100-percent oxygen cabin killed the crew; the first crew report of fire began at 23:31:04.7 GMT [A1-C001, A1-C006, A1-C011]. Scope: ignition, fire progression, cabin atmosphere, combustibles, escape, emergency response, and corrective actions, distinguishing established conditions from the unproven exact ignition source.
payload.title: Apollo 1 (AS-204) Command Module fire, 27 January 1967

payload.original: Spacecraft 012 was mated to the launch vehicle at Launch Complex 34 on 6 January 1967. [A1-C002]
Spacecraft 012 was undergoing a "Plugs Out Integrated Test" (procedure OCP FO-K-0021-1) at the time of the accident on 27 January 1967. [A1-C001]
Crew positions: Grissom was command pilot (left seat), White senior pilot (middle seat), Chaffee pilot (right seat). [A1-C003]
The Plugs-Out Test began at 12:55 GMT (7:55 a.m. EST) when power was applied to the spacecraft. [A1-C008]
After hatch installation at 19:42 GMT, a cabin purge with oxygen began at 19:45 GMT. [A1-C007]
A significant voltage transient (surge in AC Bus 2 voltage) was recorded at 23:30:54.8 GMT. [A1-C009]
Finding 1a: there was a momentary power failure at 23:30:55 GMT. [A1-C010]
The first crew report of fire began at 23:31:04.7 GMT (6:31:04.7 p.m. EST). [A1-C011]
The fire was not intense until about 23:31:12 GMT; the slow early build-up is consistent with ignition in a zone with little combustible material. [A1-C014]
The cabin ruptured at about 23:31:19 GMT at a pressure of at least 29 psia. [A1-C015]
All transmission of voice and data from the spacecraft terminated by 23:31:22.4 GMT, three seconds after rupture. [A1-C017]
The Board estimated the Command Module atmosphere was lethal by 23:31:30 GMT, five seconds after the start of the third stage. [A1-C018]
All hatches were opened and the two outer hatches removed about five minutes after the fire report, at about 23:36 GMT (Pad Leader report ~5 min 27 s after first fire report). [A1-C022]
Medical opinion based on autopsy concluded resuscitation was impossible by 23:36 GMT. [A1-C023]
The doctors estimated their arrival at the White Room at 23:45 GMT; medical support was reported available at about 23:43 GMT. [A1-C024]

payload.mechanism: Pure oxygen at above-ambient pressure makes common materials burn intensely (Finding 9, A1-C057); nylon Raschel netting, Velcro and polyurethane foam carried the flame (A1-C025 to A1-C027); the pressure rise ruptured the cabin at about 29 psia (A1-C015). This catalog assigns the root-cause role to this combined hazardous condition; the Board itself lists six conditions without ranking a root cause (A1-C064).
payload.statement: The sealed Command Module cabin, pressurized with 100-percent oxygen at 16.7 psia and containing extensive combustible materials near possible ignition sources, turned a minor ignition into a rapidly fatal fire.

payload.mechanism: Board Determination 1 and Finding 1c (A1-C030, A1-C031); the initiation probably coincided with the power interruption at 23:30:55 GMT (A1-C034).
payload.statement: The fire was most probably initiated by an electrical arc from vulnerable wiring in the lower forward left-hand equipment bay near the Environmental Control Unit; the exact source was not identified.
The specific ignition source was a chafed power cable beneath the lithium hydroxide access door.
The specific ignition source was an arc at the cover of junction box C-15-1A-52 in the extreme lower-left corner of the lower equipment bay.
Spilled water/glycol coolant initiated the fire.
The fire was initiated non-electrically: electrostatic discharge, spontaneous combustion, mechanically produced heat or a struck object.
A malfunction of an electrically powered spacecraft system or subassembly initiated the fire.
The fire was caused by sabotage.
Deficiencies in Command Module design, workmanship and quality control, including vulnerable Teflon-insulated wiring and coolant plumbing, created the ignition opportunity.
The inward-opening, multi-piece hatch could not be opened against the cabin pressure, so the crew could not escape.
The test was not classified as hazardous, so no emergency escape, rescue, fire or medical preparations were in place.
Program management problems and overconfidence from earlier pure-oxygen operations let the hazardous conditions persist unaddressed.

payload.statement: The Board report contains internal inconsistencies: a first pressure rise printed as 23:21:11 GMT, a GMT-to-EST conversion printed as 'subtract 17 hours', and a rupture quadrant read as '+Y, -Z' in the scan but '-Y, +Z' in NASA's transcription.

payload.basis: Each is a typographical inconsistency resolved by the report's own paired times and figures; recorded so the errors are not propagated.

payload.statement: Sources differ on the size of the Review Board.
Opening time of the new unified hatch is given as five seconds (SP-4205) and as seven seconds from inside and ten seconds by the pad crew (Apollo 7 press kit).

payload.basis: Both describe an outward-opening hatch openable in seconds independent of cabin overpressure; the primary press kit values are preferred.

payload.question: Which specific arc or failure ignited the fire?

payload.basis: The Board found no single ignition source and expected it will most likely never be positively identified; the evidence was destroyed by the fire (A1-C029, A1-C030, A1-C045).

payload.question: Was the 23:30:55 GMT power transient the ignition itself or an early effect of the fire?

payload.basis: The Board cautions the pre-fire transients may as easily be a result of the fire as its cause (A1-C036).

payload.question: What did the House Subcommittee on NASA Oversight's own report conclude?

payload.basis: The report was not retrieved; only a hearing excerpt was read. Its conclusions are not used.

payload.proposition: The Board's final report times (GMT) supersede the interim reports' times.

payload.reason: The Board found the most probable initiator was an electrical arc.
Board determination, fire-damage patterns and timing agree on an arc near the ECU as the most probable initiator; the exact source is a separate accepted unknown.
The test was run in 100-percent oxygen at 16.7 psia.
Board findings on atmosphere, combustibles and fire progression, reproduced by the mock-up test.
Teflon wiring insulation was vulnerable to abrasion.
Board Finding 10 on design, workmanship and quality control.
The inner hatch opened inward against cabin pressure.
Board Finding 4: the crew was never capable of emergency egress.
The test was not classified as hazardous.
Board Finding 5 and Determination 5.
Open engineering orders and an incomplete constraint list at test time.
Board Determination 11 and the Board's conclusion on neglected crew-safety questions.

payload.mechanism: A most probable electrical arc near the ECU (trigger; exact source unidentified) ignited combustibles in a sealed 100-percent oxygen cabin at 16.7 psia (root condition, as assigned by this catalog); the fire spread rapidly, the pressure rise ruptured the cabin within about 15 seconds and toxic gases killed the crew. The inward-opening hatch prevented escape and no rescue preparations existed for a test not classified as hazardous; deficient wiring and workmanship provided the ignition opportunity, and management problems let these conditions persist.
payload.outcome: Fire in Command Module 012 during the Plugs-Out Integrated Test and the death of the crew

payload.description: Remove the conditions for a rapid cabin fire: 60/40 oxygen-nitrogen launch-pad cabin atmosphere, restriction and control of combustible materials with material substitution, protective covers over wire bundles, stainless-steel oxygen lines and armored coolant solder joints.
Replace the two-piece inward-opening hatch with a unified quick-opening, outward-opening hatch that can be opened from inside or outside independent of cabin overpressure.

Classify all tests in 100-percent oxygen environments as hazardous, establish an Office of Flight Safety independent of the program office, and provide emergency procedures, equipment and training for pad tests.

payload.expectedOutcome: Full-scale boilerplate fire tests in the revised launch-pad atmosphere show fire propagation within acceptable limits.
The first crewed Block II spacecraft, carrying the changes, completes its flight with all spacecraft systems operating satisfactorily.
The unified hatch is demonstrated to open in seconds from inside and by the pad crew, independent of cabin overpressure.
payload.method: Hatch opening or egress test record

payload.residualUncertainty: The exact ignition source remains unknown and probably unknowable: several candidate arcs exist and the evidence was destroyed; whether the 23:30:55 GMT power transient was cause or effect is undetermined. The root-cause role for the oxygen-and-combustibles condition is this catalog's assignment, not the Board's ranking. The unified hatch's opening time has not been verified from a retrieved primary test record (Apollo 7 shows only that its mechanisms operated and it was used for egress), so the hatch correction remains awaiting verification and the investigation is not resolved.
payload.statement: The Apollo 1 crew died in a fire that spread rapidly through a sealed 100-percent oxygen cabin at 16.7 psia containing extensive combustibles; the fire was most probably ignited by an electrical arc from vulnerable wiring near the Environmental Control Unit, but the exact ignition source was not identified. The inward-opening hatch could not be opened against cabin pressure and the test had not been treated as hazardous. Full-scale mock-up fire tests showed the revised atmosphere and materials were firesafe, and Apollo 7 flew the changed spacecraft with its systems operating as intended.
